passages.original: CAPUT XXXVII. Anima civitas Dei. Illius cives. Consiliarii. Milites. Plebeii. Tres vires animæ secundum Platonem etmedicos. Ratio. Intelligentia. Memoria. Ape pelitus.(a) Nobilis creatura est anima. Civitas namque Dei est, de qua tam gloriosa dicta sunt (Psal. LXXXVI, 3), quod ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei facta est.
passages.english: CHAPTER XXXVII. The soul is the city of God. Its citizens. Counsellors. Soldiers. Commoners. The three powers of the soul according to Plato and the physicians. Reason. Intelligence. Memory. Appetite. The soul is a noble creature. For it is the city of God, of which such glorious things have been spoken (Ps. 86:3), because it was made to the image and likeness of God.
passages.notes: "etmedicos" read as "et medicos"; "Ape pelitus" read as "Appetitus". "(a)" is an editorial note mark and is omitted.

passages.original: Ad coelestia enim arcana penetranda ratio per se non sunicit, nisi a Deo adjuta fuerit. Tunc finis ejus, si bene viget, cum ad notitiam secretorum, quæ diu investigando quaesivit, pervenerit, intellectus seu intelligentia nuncupatur. Boethius tamen dicit intelligentiam solius Dei csse et admodum paucorum hominum ; sed horum al. terum pro alturo sare ponitur. Memoria etiam consors et cooperatrix est rationis ; quoniam sine ea ratio nee ad incognita proceucre, nee cognitorum scientiam retinere potest.
passages.english: For reason by itself is not sufficient to penetrate heavenly mysteries unless it has been helped by God. Then its end, if it is in good vigour, when it has arrived at knowledge of the secrets which it long sought by investigating, is called understanding or intelligence. Boethius, however, says that intelligence belongs to God alone and to very few men; but each of these terms is often used for the other. Memory too is the partner and co-worker of reason, since without it reason can neither advance to unknown things nor retain knowledge of things known.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "sunicit" = sufficit, "csse" = esse, "al. terum pro alturo sare" read as "alterum pro altero saepe" ("often" is conjectural), "nee" = nec, "proceucre" = procedere.

passages.original: CAPUT XLVIII. Animarum origo. Arbitrium. Ele- ctio. (b) Credimus animas non esse ab initio cum Angelis, nee sim!!! creatas, sicut Origenes fingit. Nec per coitum cum corporibus seminantur, sicut Luciferiani 1 et Cyrillus , et aliqui Latinorum præsumptores affirmant. Sed dicimus earum creationem solumomnium Creatorem nosse : corpus tautum per conjugii copulam seminari;
passages.english: CHAPTER XLVIII. The origin of souls. Choice. Election. We believe that souls did not exist from the beginning with the angels, nor were created all together, as Origen imagines. Nor are they sown along with bodies through intercourse, as the Luciferians and Cyril and some presumptuous Latin writers assert. But we say that only the Creator of all knows their creation; that the body alone is sown through the union of marriage;
passages.notes: "sim!!! " read as "simul" ("together"). "Luciferiani 1": the "1" is a footnote mark. The Cyril meant is not identified here.

passages.original: ut labamur, potesta- tis nostræ cst et ignaviæ. Solum bominem eredimus habere animam substantivam,quæ exuta corpore vivit, et sensus suos atque ingenia vivaciter tenet. Neque cum corpore moritur, ut Aratus I asserit; npque postmodum interitura , sicut Zenon dicit: quia subslantialiter vivit. Animalium vero animae non sunt substantivæ, sed cum carne ipsa carnis vivacitate nascuntur, et cum carnis morte finiuntur: et ideo nec ratione reguntur sicut Plato et Alexander putant; sed ad omnia naturæ incitamenta ducuntur. Anima humana non cum carne moritur, quia nec cum carne, ut diximus superius , seminatur : sod formato in utero matris corpore, Dei judicio creari et infundi eam diximus, ut vivat homo intus in utero,et sic procedat nativitate in mundum.
passages.english: that we fall is within our power and [due to] our sloth. We believe that man alone has a substantive soul, which lives when stripped of the body and vigorously keeps its senses and faculties. Nor does it die with the body, as Aratus asserts; nor will it perish afterwards, as Zeno says, because it lives substantially. But the souls of animals are not substantive; they are born with the flesh itself through the vitality of the flesh, and are ended with the death of the flesh; and therefore they are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander think, but are led by all the promptings of nature. The human soul does not die with the flesh, because neither, as we said above, is it sown with the flesh; but we have said that, when the body has been formed in the mother's womb, it is created and infused by God's judgement, so that the man lives within the womb and so comes forth by birth into the world.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence. "Aratus I": "I" is a footnote mark; the attribution to Aratus is unusual (the source tradition may have a different name). Alexander is unidentified (perhaps Alexander of Aphrodisias).

passages.original: Nec proprietates suas potest exercere, donce usu et experientia et alicujus doctrina incitata incipit discernere; veluti si quis cum subtili licet acie oculorum in tenebrosa detrudatur, videre tamen non potest ibi , nisi prins assuescat tenebris , vei lumcn accendatur. Unde Virgilius: Quantum non noxia corpora tardant. (Æneid. lib. 6, vers. 731.) Et licet aliæ sint actiones corporis, et aliæ animae actiones; tamen corporis vitia vel virtutes possunt esse animæ. Cum enim ad hoc sit anima data , ut illicitos carnis motus corrigat, ignoranlia illius contingunt vel negligentia.
passages.english: Nor can it exercise its own properties until, stirred by use and experience and someone's teaching, it begins to discern; just as if someone, though with keen sight, is thrust into dark places, he still cannot see there unless he first grows used to the darkness or a light is lit. Hence Virgil: "so far as harmful bodies do not slow [them]." (Aeneid 6.731.) And although the actions of the body are one thing and the actions of the soul another, yet the vices or virtues of the body can belong to the soul. For since the soul was given for this purpose, to correct the unlawful motions of the flesh, they occur through its ignorance or negligence.
passages.notes: "donce" = donec, "prins" = prius, "vei lumcn" = vel lumen, "ignoranlia" = ignorantia.
